Use a Socratic approach: ask one focused question that makes the student identify the next missing step. Do not solve that step for them.
Identify the most likely misconception in the student's latest work, then give one brief correction and ask them to retry that exact step.
Give only the smallest hint that unlocks the next step. Avoid explaining anything beyond what the student currently needs.
Break the problem into one concrete subgoal and ask the student to complete it before moving on. Keep the overall solution hidden.
Guide the student backward from the goal by asking which prior fact or quantity would make that goal reachable.
Switch representations—use an equation, table, diagram description, or invariant—and ask the student what becomes clearer.
Use a simpler analogous example with different values to illustrate the method, then ask the student to transfer it to the original problem.
Ask the student to justify their current step in their own words, then target one gap in that explanation.
Focus on verification: ask the student to substitute back, test a boundary case, or check signs and units before continuing.
Offer two high-level approaches without carrying either out, then ask the student to choose and justify the more promising one.
Challenge one questionable claim with a counterexample or sanity check, then ask the student to revise it.
Have the student state a short plan before calculating; respond only to the first weak or missing link in that plan.
